children: By AnnaMaria Andriotis and Emily Glazer

The board of Goldman Sachs has discussed a plan for David Solomon to step down as chief executive and be replaced with Chief Operating Officer John Waldron as soon as next year, according to people familiar with the matter.

Discussions have involved Waldron, who is also the bank's president, taking over the top job around the end of 2027 or in 2028, the people said. Under the plan, Solomon is likely to be executive chairman of the Goldman board for around one to two years after he steps down from the CEO role, some of the people said.
The plan requires approval by Goldman's board, which could occur in the coming months, some of the people familiar with the matter said, though the timing is fluid and subject to change.

After this article published, Goldman spokesman Tony Fratto, who initially declined to comment on succession planning, said the board regularly discusses succession and there is no definitive timeline.

The move would mark the end of Solomon's near decade atop the firm, which included a rocky period several years ago but has recently benefited from Goldman's renewed focus on its core Wall Street businesses and its stock trading near record highs.

Waldron's expected ascension to CEO presents an opening for other senior executives to move around. The company has been transitioning duties associated with Waldron's COO role to its finance chief Denis Coleman over the past year, according to people familiar with the matter.

That includes some human resources work as well as an artificial intelligence transformation Goldman calls "OneGS 3.0," that involves changing the firm's internal operating model and improving overall productivity. Coleman and Waldron have a close relationship, Goldman partners say.

Waldron's ascension would also open up the seat of president. It is unclear how this will shake out, in large part because board members are factoring in the risk of losing top executives if they don't get the title. Those executives include the co-heads of the firm's behemoth global banking and markets division Dan Dees and Ashok Varadhan and Marc Nachmann, global head of asset and wealth management.

Dees' star inside Goldman has hit new highs following several large dealmaking wins, including helping Goldman land a coveted role helping run SpaceX's IPO. Varadhan has long been the firm's markets and trading whiz while Nachmann is about four years into repositioning and expanding the firm's asset and wealth management division, a priority for the firm.
Waldron, 57, who has long eyed the CEO role, has been the heir apparent for years and board members don't want to risk delaying a transition, the people said.
Waldron explored options outside the firm a few years ago, after Solomon, 64, had made clear to top Goldman executives that he wasn't going anywhere for years.

During the last half of 2024, Goldman's board became aware of serious discussions between Waldron and Apollo Global Management, as well as other investment firms that were looking to hire him, The Wall Street Journal previously reported. The board moved to keep Waldron at Goldman in part with an $80 million retention bonus that was announced in January 2025 to stay with the firm for five more years. (Solomon received the same bonus.)
Waldron was also added to the firm's board last year.

Prior to the Apollo discussions, Waldron talked with Carlyle when the private-capital firm was looking for its next CEO. He informed higher-ups at Goldman of the discussions and was told that if he stayed, he had a good chance of becoming the next Goldman chief, the Journal previously reported. Afterward, Goldman alum Harvey Schwartz took over at Carlyle in 2023.

Solomon and Waldron have had a close relationship over the years. Both cemented their careers at the firm within its investment banking division. They arrived at Goldman more than 25 years ago, Solomon in 1999 and Waldron in 2000. Both worked at Bear Stearns earlier in their careers. After Solomon was named CEO of Goldman in 2018, Waldron was chosen as the firm's president and COO.

Solomon had a bruising stretch around 2022 to 2024 that cast his longevity as CEO into doubt among many partners. He directed an aggressive expansion of the consumer-lending business, started by his predecessor, but the effort flopped and Goldman is nearing the end of its exit from the sector having lost roughly $7 billion on a pretax basis since the beginning of 2020 on a large chunk of this business.

The firm experienced an exodus of partners, in part from frequent reorganizations of its asset-management business. Solomon's hobby of DJing had drawn criticism and negative headlines, personalizing the drama at the bank.

More recently, Solomon stopped DJing at public events, the firm has moved to prioritize and expand its two core businesses-dealmaking and markets as well as asset and wealth management-and the stock has surged. An initiative spearheaded by Solomon that incentivizes the firm's units to steer business to each other has boosted volumes across the firm, including in its investment banking and wealth businesses and its financing to a variety of corporate clients.
Goldman's stock has more than quadrupled since Solomon became CEO in October 2018 compared with a gain of about 67% for a broader index of bank stocks.

Waldron is best known for being a top dealmaker and a key client-facing asset of the firm. He has an extensive Rolodex of close relationships with the heads of large corporations and an uncanny ability to strike relationships in both the private and public sectors and with foreign government leaders that benefit the firm.

As president and COO, roles he has held since 2018, he and Solomon worked on identifying the firm's next generation of leaders. He also became a sounding board for Goldman partners and other executives who at times sought to express concern or discontent with the firm's direction-including the now-aborted plans to become a consumer lender.
